title: Methodus nova et facilis calculum variationum tractandi

deep.reconstruction:
Section 24 (continued). After treating expressions of the 'first' and 'second kind' (functions of x, y, z and the partial derivatives of z, and their variations under a parameter t, §§19–23), Euler turns to the 'third kind', meaning expressions that contain integral formulas. He says this is where the power of his method mainly shows.

When one seeks surfaces z = z(x,y) that maximize or minimize some quantity, the quantity must be an integral. Because the base over which the surface lies is a region of the horizontal (x,y)-plane, not an interval on the abscissa x, the integral is a double integral ∫∫V dx dy. In modern terms the functional is J[z] = ∬_D V(x,y,z,z_x,z_y,z_xx,…) dx dy.

Euler defines the double integral as an iterated integral. First integrate in one variable, x or y, holding the other fixed, out to the boundary of the given base. Then integrate in the remaining variable. Since it does not matter which variable is taken first, he writes ∫∫ without distinguishing the order. For details he refers to Novi Commentarii Tomus XIV, i.e. his paper E391 'De formulis integralibus duplicatis'.

The page sets up §§25–26. There the variation is dt∬(dV/dt)dx dy, written either as dt∫dx∫(dV/dt)dy or as dt∫dy∫(dV/dt)dx. The expansion of §23 is then inserted, preparing the integrations by parts that lead to the Euler–Lagrange equation (Euler–Ostrogradsky) for surfaces.
errors: No real error. The statement 'perinde est utra prius pro variabili habeatur' (it makes no difference which variable is taken first) is stated without qualification. For a non-rectangular base the limits of the inner integral depend on the outer variable and must be re-determined when the order is swapped; E391 treats this. Validity of the interchange (a Fubini-type condition) is assumed tacitly, as was usual in the 18th century.

ideas.what: Extremum problems for surfaces require a double-integral functional over a planar base region
ideas.modern_name: Multiple-integral variational problem (functional ∬_D F(x,y,u,∇u,∇²u) dx dy)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Lagrange (1760–61, Essai d'une nouvelle méthode…, minimal surfaces); systematized by Euler (E420), later Ostrogradsky, Poisson
ideas.where_published: E420 itself (Novi Comm. 16, 1771/1772); related remarks in Institutiones calculi integralis vol. III appendix (E385)

ideas.what: Double integral defined as an iterated integral, with the order of integration immaterial
ideas.where_published: E391 'De formulis integralibus duplicatis', Novi Comm. Acad. Sci. Petrop. 14 (1770)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a transitional, expository page. It introduces double integrals for surface problems and cites Euler's own earlier paper E391. Everything here is well documented in the history of multiple integrals and of the calculus of variations.
transcription_corrections: Transcription matches the image. 'neceſſaro' is a printer's typo for 'neceſſario' and is faithfully transcribed.
Footer reads 'Tom. XVI. Nou. Comm.' with signature 'G' and catchword '25.'; this is correct.
